evaluated.name: Externally Financed Tangible Expansion Without Knowledge
evaluated.hypothesis: Raising outside equity and debt to fund expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has no knowledge-based competitive advantage to deploy the capital against.
evaluated.reasoning: External financing predicts low returns partly because managers issue when overvalued, but R&D-rich firms have genuine funding needs for intangible projects that markets ration. The multiplicative rank interaction fires only when heavy external financing coincides with low R&D-to-sales, distinguishing opportunistic capital raising from knowledge-driven financing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Acceleration Minus R&D Acceleration
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm accelerating physical capital spending while simultaneously decelerating knowledge investment is late in its investment cycle and reallocating toward commoditized capacity, foreshadowing declining profitability and low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Second-difference framing captures the reallocation decision at the margin rather than the level of investment intensity, which is heavily industry-determined. Managers cut discretionary R&D first when they chase near-term capacity, so the wedge between the two accelerations is an early-warning composition signal not visible in either investment or intangible level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Goodwill-Purged Knowledge Capital Tilt
evaluated.expression: SUB(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(intan, 0), COALESCE(gdwl, 0)), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)), at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(ppegt, at), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms shifting their capital stock toward identifiable, non-goodwill intangibles and accumulated R&D, and away from gross physical plant, are migrating to knowledge-based production whose value is conservatively accounted and slow to be priced.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique is addressed by explicitly subtracting goodwill from `intan`, so the numerator captures patents, developed technology and licensed know-how plus a three-year organic R&D stock, rather than the deal premium that signals overpaying acquirers. Differencing against the change in the gross PP&E share nets out pure scale effects and isolates the tangible-versus-intangible composition shift, keeping the positive sign internally consistent with the goodwill-is-bad logic of the accepted acquisition signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Physical Expansion During Own-History R&D Retrenchment
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross plant expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has simultaneously pushed its own R&D intensity to a five-year low, indicating capital is being redirected from innovation into commoditized capacity.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the earlier validator failure by anchoring the investment leg on gross PP&E (an investment-exclusive variable) rather than total assets, while the intangible leg is a within-firm time-series position, so a chronically high-R&D firm at its own knowledge trough is flagged as strongly as a perennial non-innovator. Both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks, so the product is monotone and cannot flip sign, and the short leg concentrates on firms scaling hard capacity precisely as they disinvest in knowledge.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Plant Growth Deflated by Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: The overinvestment penalty attaches to physical capital accumulation measured against the firm's true (tangible plus unbooked knowledge) capital base, so identical dollar plant additions are far more aggressive for firms with no R&D stock than for knowledge-rich firms.
evaluated.reasoning: The intangible theme enters through the deflator rather than a multiplicative weight, keeping the construct monotone with a strictly positive denominator and no sign-flip risk; this is the scaling-design repair of the earlier rejected idea, now grounded in ppent rather than assets. It isolates a clean question the archive has not answered: whether capitalizing R&D into the denominator sharpens the physical-investment penalty relative to conventional asset scaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Buy Versus Build Investment Mix
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that source growth by purchasing other companies rather than by building internal knowledge capital are paying acquisition premia for capability they cannot generate organically, and subsequently underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The measure is a bounded share of the firm's total growth budget, so it avoids the sparse-goodwill and additive-rank problems of the earlier acquisition proposal while keeping the buy-versus-build contrast explicit inside a single investment budget constraint. Both zero-acquisition and zero-R&D firms are economically meaningful corners here, so the COALESCE convention is substantive rather than a coverage patch.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Idle Cash Not Converted Into Knowledge
evaluated.hypothesis: Large cash balances are rewarded when they fund an innovation pipeline but are an agency liability when the firm has no knowledge investment to fund, so cash-rich non-innovators underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests a financial-slack channel distinct from the archive's external-financing winner: there the interaction was about raising capital, here it is about hoarding it without a knowledge use, which reverses the usual positive cash-R&D pricing result documented for innovative firms. The three-year cumulative R&D stock smooths lumpy annual reporting so the conditioning leg measures a sustained innovation program rather than a single-year expense.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Labor Bloat With Retreating Research
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose headcount grows faster than revenue while they simultaneously cut research intensity are scaling low-productivity labor at the same time they abandon the innovation that could justify it, and this joint divergence predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are changed relative to the flagged version: the active leg is now headcount growth in excess of sales growth, a labor-productivity deterioration measure rather than the published hiring-rate anomaly, and the gate is a within-firm decline in R&D intensity rather than the archive winner's cross-sectional low-R&D level. The mechanism is a divergence between two simultaneous input decisions — adding people while withdrawing knowledge spend — which neither the labor anomaly nor R&D intensity captures alone, and treating unreported R&D as a constant zero places non-innovators at a neutral middle rank instead of dropping them.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power
evaluated.hypothesis: Heavy reinvestment in physical capacity is value-destructive precisely for firms lacking an intangible moat, proxied by a persistently thin gross margin, because added capacity in a commoditized product market cannot earn rents.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons both the change-of-share framing that made the flagged proposal a near-restatement of the capex-minus-R&D acceleration signal and the unstable COALESCE(xad, 0) term whose appearing-and-disappearing reporting corrupted a differenced measure. It measures the intangible side through realized pricing power — a three-year average gross margin, which is the economic output of brand and know-how rather than its accounting input — so it tests whether the moat, not the R&D line item, is what conditions the investment penalty, and it applies to the full sample including firms that never report R&D.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial Acquirer Without Internal Research
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that have sustained a five-year program of buying growth while spending nothing on internal knowledge creation are rollups whose reported expansion is purchased rather than earned, and they persistently underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's Buy-Versus-Build mix delivered the largest FF5 alpha (-4.6%, t = -4.2) but a negligible Fama-MacBeth slope, which is the signature of a one-year, small-denominator ratio whose tails drive the portfolio while the cross-sectional slope is swamped by noise; replacing single-year flows with five-year cumulative spending scaled by sales gives a persistent state variable that should register cross-sectionally as well. This tests whether the buy-versus-build effect is a durable strategic-posture attribute rather than a transaction-year artifact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Build Without Pricing Power
evaluated.hypothesis: Stocking inventory faster than revenue grows is a demand-forecasting error whose cost is highest for firms without brand or product differentiation, since a commodity producer must clear excess stock through price cuts that destroy margin.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power was the only signal strong on both dimensions (fmb -3.1, alpha -3.0%, t = -2.9), indicating that the realized-moat gate measured by gross margin carries information the R&D expense line does not; this extends that gate to working-capital investment, an investment channel unlikely to be spanned by the FF5 investment factor built on asset growth. Netting out sales growth ensures the signal captures unwanted accumulation rather than ordinary scaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that expand revenue without expanding gross plant, and that have an accumulated R&D stock capable of explaining how, are monetizing unbooked knowledge capital whose scalability the market underprices.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal so far is short-side and negative-signed, leaving the long side of the intangibles story untested; this construct is deliberately built on revenue growth rather than asset growth so that it is not simply the mirror image of the FF5 investment factor, which absorbed the plant-growth signals that had strong slopes but zero alpha. The interaction is essential: sales growth without plant growth is ambiguous alone, and R&D intensity alone is a documented level effect, but jointly they identify knowledge-driven operating leverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Erratic Capex Without Knowledge Anchor
evaluated.hypothesis: Unstable physical investment reflects reactive, opportunity-chasing capital allocation, and it is most damaging in firms with no sustained knowledge program to give the spending strategic direction.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces a second-moment investment channel absent from the archive, which has tested only levels, changes and accelerations, and the FF5 investment factor prices the level of investment rather than its instability, so the spread has a plausible route to surviving as alpha. The knowledge stock enters as the anchor that distinguishes lumpy but purposeful capacity building in innovative firms from erratic allocation in firms with no research program.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Purchased Goodwill Overhang Versus Self-Built Knowledge
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose capital base consists mostly of goodwill bought in past deals, in excess of the knowledge capital they built themselves, carry an overhang of capitalized acquisition premia that must be written down or earned back, and they underperform firms of the same size whose intangible base is self-generated.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the flow budget share entirely and moves to a stock-composition construct, which repairs the exact pathology the critic identified: the denominator is net plant plus two non-negative intangible stocks, so it is strictly positive and cannot approach zero or flip sign, and the whole measure is bounded in the interval from minus one to one without winsorizing. The economic content also changes from a single-year allocation decision to the accumulated composition of the firm's capital — purchased versus organically created intangibles measured against the physical base — which is the durable state variable the one-year Buy-Versus-Build ratio only glimpsed in transaction years.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Plant Contraction With Research Intensification
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm simultaneously shrinking its physical capital base and raising research intensity is executing a deliberate pivot from replicable hard assets toward knowledge capital, and because the R&D is expensed while the plant reduction is visible, reported fundamentals understate the transition and returns are subsequently high.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's two objections are both structural and both fixed: the horizons are now matched — a one-year plant change against a one-year change in research intensity — and the intangible leg is a within-firm change rather than a level, so the signal is orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly and cannot be a monotone transform of it. The interaction is essential because plant contraction alone is often distress and rising research intensity alone is often a sales collapse in the denominator, whereas their conjunction identifies genuine reallocation; both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks so the product is monotone in each channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquiring Without A Moat
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisitions destroy value mainly for firms that have no pricing power of their own, because a low-margin consolidator is buying scale in a commoditized market rather than acquiring differentiated capability it can monetize.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows two separately successful families — the acquisition channel, which delivers the largest alphas, and the realized-moat gate measured by sustained gross margin, which is the only conditioning variable that has produced joint cross-sectional and portfolio strength — and this crosses them for the first time. Replacing the R&D-expense gate with the margin gate also broadens the test to the majority of firms that never report R&D, where a rank on COALESCE(xrd, 0) is uninformative.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Freshly Built Plant Without Knowledge
evaluated.hypothesis: A high ratio of net to gross plant means the firm's physical capital is young, the cumulative product of a recent build-out, and that embedded capacity commitment is a liability rather than an asset for firms with no knowledge capital to differentiate what the capacity produces.
evaluated.reasoning: Capital vintage is a stock characteristic rather than an investment flow, so unlike the plant-growth signals that scored fmb -5.0 with zero alpha it is not a near-relative of the CMA asset-growth factor, which is the most plausible explanation for that earlier absorption. The interaction is necessary because young plant is neutral or good for a differentiated innovator retooling for a new product, and damaging only for a commodity producer that has locked in replicable capacity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt Against Non-Collateralizable Knowledge
evaluated.hypothesis: Knowledge capital cannot be pledged or liquidated, so leverage carried against an intangible-heavy asset base creates a fragile financing structure that forces pro-cyclical research cuts and depresses subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This flips the sign convention of the archive's R&D gate — high research intensity is the risk amplifier here rather than the protective factor — which makes it a genuinely different economic claim about asset-liability matching rather than another restatement of the R&D premium. It also opens the capital-structure channel on the debt side, whereas the archive's financing evidence comes only from gross issuance flows.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Goodwill Write-Down After Acquisitive Growth
evaluated.hypothesis: When a serial acquirer's goodwill balance falls, management has conceded that previously capitalized acquisition premia were illusory, and because impairments are lagged and partial the market continues to over-value the remaining acquired intangibles.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests the realization stage of the acquisition story rather than the spending stage, a mechanism absent from the archive: the conditioning restricts the goodwill decline to firms with a documented five-year acquisition program, distinguishing genuine impairment from routine divestiture or currency translation. If the acquisition family's alpha is really about overpaid intangibles, the impairment event should time the underperformance more sharply than the spending level does.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Knowledge-Backed Gross Profit Scaling
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that expand gross profit without expanding plant, and that hold a research stock capable of explaining the source of that expansion, are converting unbooked knowledge capital into rents the market has not capitalized.
evaluated.reasoning: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling is the archive's only joint-strength long-side result (fmb 2.4, alpha 2.8%, t 2.5), and the critic's diagnosis was that its raw sales-growth leg fights the signal because unprofitable revenue growth is itself a negative predictor; replacing sales growth with gross-profit growth keeps the asset-light scaling concept while filtering out margin-dilutive expansion. This is a targeted quality refinement of a proven mechanism rather than a new template, and it should improve both the slope and the alpha if the original leg was contaminated as diagnosed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payback On Combined Hard And Soft Investment
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), LAG(SUB(sale, cogs), 3)), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: Treating research spending as investment alongside capital expenditure, the gross profit a firm has actually generated per dollar of its total three-year hard-plus-soft outlay measures the realized productivity of its investment program, and high-payback firms are undervalued because the R&D half of the outlay was expensed and never appeared as capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic is right that the tie-mass diagnosis was wrong — Buy Versus Build was already continuous and still scored fmb -0.77 — so the correct reading is that acquisition intensity simply has no cross-sectional slope because it discriminates only within a small extreme corner, and a third denominator variant of that same construct would be wasted budget. This slot therefore moves to an untested mechanism with continuous variation across the whole sample: not the composition of investment, which the archive has probed repeatedly, but the realized payback on the two investment types pooled into one outlay, which is precisely the quantity distorted by expensing R&D and therefore the most likely source of a joint slope and alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising gross profit per employee achieved without expanding physical plant is the fingerprint of organizational and human capital — intangible assets that never enter the balance sheet — and firms displaying it earn abnormal returns as the productivity gain proves durable.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has proxied intangibles only through R&D spending, goodwill and gross margin, never through labor productivity, even though human and organizational capital is the largest unbooked intangible category for most firms; employment is broadly reported, so this avoids the zero-mass problem that flattens the R&D-gated signals. The interaction is necessary because profit per employee can rise simply through capital substitution, and requiring flat or falling gross plant isolates the intangible source from the mechanization source.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Expansion Into Eroding Margins
evaluated.hypothesis: Building capacity is most destructive when the firm's competitive position is actively deteriorating, so a multi-year downward margin trajectory identifies over-expansion far better than a low but stable margin level, which may simply reflect a structurally thin-margin business model.
evaluated.reasoning: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power is the archive's best short-side joint result, but its level-based gate necessarily confounds industry cost structure with moat erosion, and the critic flagged that it may re-express the gross-profitability anomaly. Replacing the moat level with the moat trajectory isolates that specific design choice while making the economic claim sharper: it is losing pricing power, not having thin margins, that turns investment into value destruction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Research Decay With Capacity Ramp
evaluated.hypothesis: An innovator whose current research spending has fallen well below its own five-year norm while it accelerates physical investment is harvesting a depleting knowledge stock, and the market continues to price the firm on an innovation profile it no longer sustains.
evaluated.reasoning: Every R&D leg in the archive is either a cross-sectional level or a one-year change, both of which conflate structural non-innovators with genuine retrenchers; normalizing current R&D by the firm's own five-year average makes the measure scale-free, orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly, and interpretable only within the innovator population where the depletion story applies. The capacity ramp supplies the reallocation evidence, distinguishing a firm cutting research because it is dying from one deliberately shifting its capital toward replicable hard assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Improving Productivity Of Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: When the capital base is measured correctly — plant plus inventory plus the capitalized research stock that accounting expenses away — an improvement in gross profit per dollar of that true capital signals rising economic productivity that reported returns on assets understate for research-intensive firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than recombining two archive legs, this transfers the one deflator idea that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (knowledge-inclusive capital, fmb -5.0 when applied to investment) onto an entirely different quantity, profitability, where it has never been tested, and it does so as a change so the sort is not simply the gross-profitability level that RMW already prices. The interaction is intrinsic to the construct: for a plant-heavy firm the denominator is almost all tangible and the measure reduces to conventional capital productivity, while for a research-heavy firm the expensed knowledge stock dominates and the measure re-prices the firm on capital the balance sheet never recorded.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Irreversible Capacity Under Demand Uncertainty
evaluated.hypothesis: Physical capacity is irreversible while research spending can be throttled year to year, so firms facing volatile demand that nevertheless commit their investment budget to hard assets are exercising real options badly and earn lower subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic is right that the acquisition family is saturated — four different gates produced nearly identical alphas with flat slopes, which is evidence the aqc leg alone drives it — so this slot moves to an untested channel: the irreversibility-versus-flexibility distinction between tangible and intangible investment, which is the deepest economic difference between the two themes and one the archive has never exploited. The interaction is indispensable, since a hard-asset investment mix is perfectly sensible under stable demand and only becomes a real-options error when demand volatility is high.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer-Relative Inventory Build Without Peer-Relative Moat
evaluated.hypothesis: Excess inventory accumulation signals value destruction when the firm's pricing power is weak relative to its own industry peers, because a below-peer margin identifies a genuine competitive deficit rather than the structurally thin margins that characterize entire distribution-heavy sectors.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons advertising entirely, accepting the critic's point that COALESCE(xad, 0) turns the measure into a consumer-industry reporting indicator, and redirects the slot to repairing a specific documented divergence: Inventory Build Without Pricing Power delivered alpha -4.9% with t -4.18 but a Fama-MacBeth slope of only -0.44, exactly the pattern expected if the sort is largely a stable sector tilt that a portfolio spread monetizes but a cross-sectional slope cannot detect. Industry-neutralizing both legs converts the signal from a sector bet into a within-peer-group competitive-position measure, so if the slope becomes significant while the alpha survives, we learn the moat mechanism is real at the firm level rather than an industry artifact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard Capital Stock Under Demand Uncertainty
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters under volatile demand is not only this year's allocation decision but the accumulated stock of sunk physical capital relative to flexible knowledge capital, because a firm already locked into plant cannot contract when demand disappoints.
evaluated.reasoning: Irreversible Capacity Under Demand Uncertainty is now the archive's best joint result (fmb -2.62, alpha -5.2%, t -3.74), and the first question for consolidation is whether the effect is a flow decision or a state of commitment; this replaces the one-year investment mix with the corresponding capital-stock composition while holding the uncertainty leg fixed. A stock formulation is also mechanically more stable than a single-year capex ratio, so it should raise coverage-quality and the cross-sectional slope if the commitment interpretation is right.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Externally Financed Hard Investment Mix
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Raising outside capital is most damaging when the proceeds are committed to replicable physical capacity rather than to knowledge creation, because investors fund a sunk expansion whose competitive advantage any rival can duplicate.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's oldest joint winner paired external financing with the absence of R&D relative to sales, but the uncertainty result shows the hard-versus-soft budget share is a sharper and better-scaled expression of the same underlying distinction, with no zero-mass problem in the denominator; substituting it tests whether the financing penalty is about lacking knowledge or about where the money goes. This isolates a single well-defined design choice on a mechanism already validated on both metrics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Knowledge-Intensive Labor Productivity Gains
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising gross profit per employee at research-intensive firms is evidence that accumulated knowledge capital is being converted into human-capital productivity, a combination the market underprices because neither the research stock nor the productivity gain appears on the balance sheet.
evaluated.reasoning: Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant produced a strong slope of +3.03 but a wrong-signed alpha of -2.2%, and the diagnosis is the second leg: ranking on falling gross plant loads the long portfolio with shrinking, distressed firms whose FF5 exposures turn the spread negative. Replacing the plant-contraction gate with the research-stock gate keeps the human-capital mechanism, removes the distress tilt, and reuses the conditioning variable that carries the archive's only reliable long-side alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unstable Research Program In A Capital-Heavy Firm
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that runs its research budget erratically while carrying a heavy sunk physical capital base has neither a credible innovation program nor the flexibility to adapt, and this combination of unreliable intangible investment and rigid tangible commitment predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the acquisition channel entirely, accepting the critic's evidence that five draws from that well all recover the same acquirer main effect, and instead moves the second-moment idea to the intangible side, which the archive has never tested — every volatility measure so far has been on capex. It complements rather than repeats Erratic Capex Without Knowledge Anchor, because there instability was measured in the hard channel and the gate was the R&D level, whereas here instability is measured in the knowledge program itself and the gate is the rigidity of the asset base.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Thin Liquidity Against Investment Commitments Under Uncertainty
evaluated.hypothesis: Volatile demand is dangerous specifically for firms whose cash reserves are small relative to the scale of the hard and soft investment programs they have committed to, because a revenue trough then forces abandonment of projects at the worst possible time.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic is correct that reversing the mix leg was an exact rank reversal contributing only the uncertainty main effect, so this replaces it with an economically independent second dimension — the liquidity buffer measured against three years of combined tangible and intangible outlays — that supplies the funding mechanism explaining why uncertainty punishes committed investors. It also rehabilitates the cash channel, which failed in Idle Cash Not Converted Into Knowledge because cash was ranked in isolation rather than against the investment obligations it must cover.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard Investment Mix Without Pricing Power
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that spend their investment budget on replicable physical capacity while lacking any pricing power are adding capital to a business that cannot earn rents on it, and the resulting value destruction is priced only with a lag.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the poorly specified option-conversion idea, whose predicted sign fought the documented R&D premium, with a sharply signed construct in which both legs point the same way and the interaction is required: a hard investment mix is unremarkable for a firm with a durable margin, and a thin margin is unremarkable for a firm investing in knowledge. It joins the archive's two best-behaved legs for the first time — the hard-versus-soft budget share that carried the -5.2% uncertainty alpha and the sustained-margin moat gate that carried the strongest short-side slope — with full-sample coverage and no zero-mass denominator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Research Instability Normalized By Scale
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(VOL(RATIO(xrd, sale), 5), MA(RATIO(xrd, sale), 3))), RANK(RATIO(ppent, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Genuine instability in a research program is the variability of research intensity relative to its own average level, and an erratic innovation effort inside a capital-heavy firm signals an allocation process with neither strategic direction nor flexibility.
evaluated.reasoning: Unstable Research Program In A Capital-Heavy Firm came out significantly wrong-signed (fmb +2.24, alpha +2.1%), and the diagnosis is clean: raw VOL of R&D intensity scales with its level, so the leg was proxying for the R&D-intensity premium rather than for instability. Dividing by the three-year mean converts it into a coefficient of variation that is orthogonal to intensity by construction, which turns a failed signal into a real test of whether inconsistency, as opposed to magnitude, of knowledge investment is punished.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Ramp Funded By Research Cuts
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm raises capital spending in the same year it cuts research dollars, it is financing bricks by sacrificing knowledge, and the resulting shift toward replicable assets predicts low returns regardless of the level of either budget.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than averaging two archived gates, this measures the substitution event itself in dollars, normalized by a smoothed revenue base, so a firm that raises both budgets or cuts both scores near zero and only genuine reallocation registers. It is distinct from the archived acceleration difference, which compared second differences of asset-scaled ratios and was dominated by capex noise, and from all the mix shares, which are level constructs that cannot see the direction of the swap.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peak-Chasing Irreversible Investment
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms commit irreversible capacity precisely when their own demand growth is at a five-year high, extrapolating a peak that mean-reverts, and the resulting sunk capital earns poor returns once demand normalizes.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a different economic claim from the archived uncertainty result, not a functional-form variant of it: there the conditioning was the dispersion of demand, here it is the firm's position in its own demand cycle, which identifies the extrapolation error rather than the risk exposure. The interaction matters because building at a demand peak is defensible for a firm whose investment is flexible research spending and destructive for one sinking the same budget into plant.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Productivity Gains With Stable Demand
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising gross profit per employee is a durable intangible capability only when the firm's demand base is stable, since stable revenue is itself evidence of customer capital, whereas the same productivity jump in a volatile business is a cyclical artifact that will reverse.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a lookback tweak on the archived labor-productivity signal but a substitution of its conditioning variable, replacing research intensity with demand stability, which reads low sales volatility as customer capital rather than as low risk. It also completes the archive's most productive short-side family from the long side: if committed hard investment under volatile demand earns -5.2%, the symmetric prediction is that intangible productivity gains under stable demand should earn a positive abnormal return, and testing it directly is more informative than another gate on R&D.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Efficiency From Rising Research
evaluated.hypothesis: Process and supply-chain knowledge shows up first as faster inventory turns, so a firm that is simultaneously raising research intensity and accelerating inventory turnover is converting intangible investment into operational efficiency the market has not priced.
evaluated.reasoning: The inventory channel has only ever been tested on the short side of this archive, as unwanted stock accumulation, and this uses it as the observable output of process innovation instead, which is a genuinely different economic reading of the same variable. Neither leg is spanned by the FF5 factors — inventory turnover growth is not asset growth and research-intensity change is not profitability — which addresses the concern that margin-improvement plus low-capex sorts merely restate CMA and RMW.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Asset-Light Profit Scaling In Skill-Deep Firms
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross profit growing faster than physical plant is most informative at firms with deep human capital, measured as research dollars invested per employee, because there the scaling is powered by knowledge embodied in people rather than by capacity utilization.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that putting employment in the denominator of both legs makes the interaction load on headcount reduction, so employment now appears only in the conditioning leg while the active leg is the archive's validated asset-light gross-profit scaling measure. This isolates one clean question: whether human-capital depth is a better conditioning variable than research intensity scaled by sales on the archive's strongest long-side mechanism, with no mechanical layoff channel connecting the two legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Reallocation Deflated By Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful size of a hard-for-soft reallocation is measured against the firm's existing capital base — plant plus accumulated knowledge — rather than against revenue, because it is the capital stock the reallocation is reshaping.
evaluated.reasoning: The champion signal deflates by smoothed sales, which mixes the reallocation with the firm's margin structure and asset turnover, so this isolates the deflator as a single design choice using a strictly positive, slow-moving denominator that directly represents the two capital types being traded off. It also connects the champion to the archive's other high-slope construction, the knowledge-inclusive capital deflator, which produced fmb -5.0 in a different application.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Total Irreversible Commitment Swap
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisitions and capital expenditure are both irreversible commitments, so the relevant reallocation is the change in total sunk spending net of the change in flexible research spending, and firms swapping into either hard channel while cutting knowledge investment underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This brings the acquisition channel — which produced the archive's largest alphas but never a cross-sectional slope — into the one construct that does have a slope, not as another gate but as a component of a single budget aggregate, which is the first specification in which deal spending enters additively rather than as a zero-inflated conditioning rank. If the aggregate outperforms the capex-only champion, the irreversibility interpretation is confirmed and acquisitions are shown to matter through commitment rather than through a separate acquirer effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard-Tilted Budget Relative To Own History
evaluated.hypothesis: What identifies a strategic tilt toward bricks is not this year's change but whether the firm's hard-minus-soft spending gap now sits at the top of its own five-year range, a state measure that is immune to industry spending norms and to one-off capital projects.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a differencing-window tweak of the champion but a different object entirely: a within-firm position measure of the spending gap in levels rather than a difference of flows, which avoids the critic's point that a three-year difference of an annual flow mixes level drift with reallocation. Because each firm is benchmarked against itself, the sort carries no cross-sectional capital-intensity tilt, so a surviving alpha would show the reallocation effect is a firm-level regime change rather than a comparison between capital-heavy and knowledge-heavy businesses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funded Research Tilt With Profit Delivery
evaluated.hypothesis: Shifting the budget from capacity toward research is a bullish signal only when the firm's gross profit is simultaneously growing, since the same shift at a shrinking firm is capital rationing under distress rather than a deliberate investment in knowledge.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than blending two correlated scaling measures under an unchanged gate, this addresses a specific unresolved question about the archive's champion: its long tail pools deliberate soft-tilting firms with distressed firms that simply cannot fund capex, and requiring contemporaneous gross-profit growth separates them. It is the first construct to use the reallocation measure as the active long-side leg, and it makes a falsifiable prediction — that the champion's long side is stronger once distress cases are screened out.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Knowledge Deepening Per Worker
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising research dollars per employee means the firm is deepening the knowledge embedded in its workforce rather than merely adding bodies, and because this human-capital investment is expensed and invisible, the market underprices it.
evaluated.reasoning: The contamination the critic identified is removed by construction: there is no rank product, so the signal does not load on the negative hiring main effect, and employment enters both numerator and deflator symmetrically so the measure is a scale-free comparison of research per head against revenue per head. Coverage stays broad because a firm with no research program has a genuine zero change in research per worker and sits at the neutral center rather than being dropped.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital Composition Drifting Toward Plant
evaluated.hypothesis: The consequence of repeated hard-for-soft reallocation is a capital base whose knowledge share is shrinking year after year, and this slow drift of composition toward replicable physical assets predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the exhausted three-year margin gate, which the critic correctly notes has delivered nearly identical alphas with flat slopes across four different investment legs and is most likely restating gross profitability, and instead asks whether the champion's flow effect shows up in the stock of capital it produces. The measure is a bounded share change with a strictly positive denominator, so it is far less tail-sensitive than the flow difference, and comparing the two tells us whether the market misprices the reallocation event or the accumulated composition it creates.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Irreversible Commitment Gap At Own-History Extreme
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is most exposed when its total sunk commitment — capital expenditure plus acquisition spending, net of flexible research spending — sits at the top of its own five-year range, because that is the point at which the firm has locked in the most irreversible capital it has ever carried relative to its revenue base.
evaluated.reasoning: Gen 7 produced two independent improvements on the champion reallocation idea, the own-history state formulation (fmb -5.71, alpha -4.8%, Sharpe -0.82) and the inclusion of acquisitions in the hard budget (fmb -4.81), and this is the one specification that tests whether they are complementary rather than substitutes. Because TS_RANK benchmarks each firm against itself, the lumpiness of acquisition spending that threatened the flow version is absorbed into the firm's own history rather than creating cross-sectional tail outliers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Tilt State With Profit Growth
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose spending gap has moved to the knowledge-tilted end of its own five-year history while its gross profit is still growing is deliberately funding innovation out of a healthy business, not rationing capital under distress.
evaluated.reasoning: Funded Research Tilt With Profit Delivery was the strongest long-side result ever recorded here (fmb 5.15, alpha +4.9%, t 4.99), and the parallel short-side evidence says the own-history state dominates the one-year flow difference, so substituting the state for the flow in the long-side construct is the natural consolidation and it holds the profit-delivery screen fixed for a clean comparison. Both legs remain non-negative ranks, so the product stays monotone and the distress cases that would otherwise pollute the knowledge-tilted tail are screened out by the profit requirement.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Broad Intangible Budget Including Advertising
evaluated.hypothesis: Brand building is intangible investment of the same economic kind as research — expensed, flexible, and value-relevant — so the hard-versus-soft spending gap should be measured against total soft investment rather than research alone.
evaluated.reasoning: Advertising has never been usefully tested in this archive because cross-sectional constructions turned it into a consumer-industry reporting indicator, but inside a within-firm TS_RANK the comparison is always the same firm against itself, which is the one setting where the reporting-population problem does not bite. If the broad-soft version matches or beats the research-only champion, the mechanism is about flexibility versus irreversibility of investment generally rather than about research specifically.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard Tilt Both Absolutely And Relative To Own History
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: The most exposed firms are those whose spending gap is hard-tilted both against their industry-wide peer distribution and against their own five-year history, since a high absolute commitment that is also unusual for the firm identifies a fresh, aggressive shift rather than a stable business model.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's own argument establishes that TS_RANK strips out all cross-firm heterogeneity, which means the champion discards the level information entirely and cannot distinguish a chronically capital-intensive firm at its own peak from a knowledge-heavy firm making the same relative move; adding the cross-sectional rank restores that orthogonal dimension rather than adjusting a deflator that leaves the within-firm ordering nearly unchanged. This is the only way to test whether the two rankings carry complementary information, and SUMRANK keeps both components bounded so neither dominates through outliers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Externally Funded Hard Tilt State
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A shift to the firm's most hard-tilted spending posture is far more damaging when it is financed by newly raised outside capital, because internally funded capacity building is disciplined by cash generation while externally funded building is not.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic is right that conditioning the hard-tilt state on gross-profit decline is algebraically almost the mirror of conditioning the soft-tilt state on gross-profit growth, so this replaces the profit dimension with an economically independent one — the funding source — which the archive has separately validated (external financing paired with the hard investment mix produced fmb -2.76, alpha -3.2%, Sharpe -0.26). The question it answers is new and sharp: whether the reallocation penalty is an overinvestment story about where money is spent or a financing story about where the money came from.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Plant Stock At Own-History Peak Against Knowledge-Inclusive Scale
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm's physical capital base reaches its own five-year high relative to the combined scale of its revenue and its accumulated knowledge capital, the accumulated overbuild is at its most extreme and subsequent returns are low.
evaluated.reasoning: The degeneracy the critic identified is removed because the denominator now contains a smoothed revenue term, so the ratio varies through time for firms that report no research and they are ranked on their own genuine capital-intensity history instead of piling at a constant extreme. The construct still tests the stock analogue of the champion — accumulated physical commitment measured against a knowledge-inclusive scale — while retaining the low-turnover, slow-moving portfolio composition that makes it a useful contrast with the flow-based signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard Tilt Against Gross Profit Capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: The burden of a hard-tilted budget should be judged against the profit stream that must fund and service it, not against revenue, because a given capacity commitment is far heavier for a thin-margin firm than for a firm earning large rents on each sales dollar.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly rejected a capital-stock deflator because a near-constant denominator leaves the within-firm ordering unchanged, but smoothed gross profit varies substantially through time and encodes margin compression, so this deflator genuinely alters which years rank as extreme for a given firm. It also folds the pricing-power information that produced repeated short-side alphas into the champion construct without adding a separate margin gate, which the archive has shown to contribute alpha but no slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hard Tilt State Under Demand Uncertainty
evaluated.hypothesis: Reaching one's most hard-tilted spending posture is most damaging when demand is volatile, because irreversible capital committed into an unstable revenue stream cannot be unwound when the trough arrives.
evaluated.reasoning: Demand uncertainty paired with the hard-soft investment mix produced the largest short-side alpha before the reallocation family appeared (-5.2%, t -3.74) and remains the only conditioning variable with a real-options rationale, whereas the external-financing gate tested in gen 8 preserved the slope but cut the alpha to -1.9%, indicating financing is not where the mispricing lives. Substituting the far stronger own-history state for the mix leg is the natural final test of whether uncertainty amplifies the champion mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Tilt State With Rising Labor Productivity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5))), RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A knowledge-tilted budget is validated not by aggregate profit growth, which can come from scale or acquisitions, but by rising gross profit per employee, which shows the intangible investment is raising the productivity of the people who carry it.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's long-side evidence rests on two different confirmations of intangible payoff — aggregate gross-profit growth and labor-productivity growth, the latter producing alpha of +4.5% with t 4.32 — and only the first has been paired with the reallocation state, leaving open whether the long-side result is a plain growth effect or a genuine productivity effect. Because per-employee profit growth is scale-free, this specification is far less exposed to the size and growth tilts that could be inflating the aggregate-profit version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Jump Into A Hard-Tilted Regime
evaluated.hypothesis: What the market misprices is the transition itself — a firm moving from the knowledge-tilted part of its own history to the capacity-tilted part within a single year — rather than the standing level of the tilt.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has established that both the flow event and the state level are priced, but not whether the state's predictive content comes from its position or from the recent movement in that position, and differencing the within-firm rank isolates the regime change while automatically neutralizing each firm's structural capital intensity. It is a distinct object from the flow reallocation ratio, which is denominated in dollars and dominated by large projects, whereas this is a bounded movement in percentile space that treats a small but decisive shift in a stable firm as informative.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory-Inclusive Commitment Tilt State
evaluated.hypothesis: Stock built for future sale is a commitment of the same economic kind as plant — cash sunk into physical goods that can only be recovered by selling them, often at a discount — so the relevant hard budget is capital expenditure plus inventory accumulation measured against flexible research spending.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a composition test of the hard side of the budget rather than a blend of two archived signals, and it is the direct analogue of the acquisition-inclusive test that proved informative in gen 8: there deal spending was folded in additively and slightly weakened the result, telling us the mechanism is not about acquirers, and here the same question is asked of working-capital commitment, which the archive has only ever tested as a standalone leg with a margin gate. Within-firm ranking keeps the lumpy inventory change benchmarked against the firm's own history rather than against structurally inventory-heavy peers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Tilt State With Funding To Sustain It
evaluated.hypothesis: A knowledge-tilted budget only creates value if the firm has the liquidity to carry the research program through a downturn, so cash relative to revenue, not current profit growth, is the condition that separates a credible innovation commitment from one that will be abandoned.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic is right that re-screening the soft tilt on gross-profit growth adds no new economics, so this replaces the screen with a forward-looking funding condition: research is a multi-year commitment that must be financed through revenue troughs, and cash is the balance-sheet evidence that the firm can honour it. This also rehabilitates a channel that failed in isolation — cash ranked against R&D intensity produced nothing — by giving it the role for which it is economically suited, validating the durability of a reallocation rather than proxying for innovation itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill-Led vs Organic Intangible Investment
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose intangible base expands through purchased goodwill rather than internally generated R&D are overpaying acquirers whose "investment" adds no productive knowledge capital, and they subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: Goodwill accretion is an investment flow that is booked at transaction prices reflecting managerial optimism, while R&D is an expensed, conservatively accounted knowledge flow that is systematically undervalued. Ranking the two channels against each other isolates acquisition-driven intangible growth from organic intangible creation, an interaction that neither the asset-growth anomaly nor the R&D-intensity anomaly captures alone. Unreported R&D is treated as zero because non-reporting firms genuinely spend nothing on formal R&D.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Externally Financed Tangible Expansion Without Knowledge
considered.hypothesis: Raising outside equity and debt to fund expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has no knowledge-based competitive advantage to deploy the capital against.
considered.reasoning: External financing predicts low returns partly because managers issue when overvalued, but R&D-rich firms have genuine funding needs for intangible projects that markets ration. The multiplicative rank interaction fires only when heavy external financing coincides with low R&D-to-sales, distinguishing opportunistic capital raising from knowledge-driven financing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex Acceleration Minus R&D Acceleration
considered.hypothesis: A firm accelerating physical capital spending while simultaneously decelerating knowledge investment is late in its investment cycle and reallocating toward commoditized capacity, foreshadowing declining profitability and low returns.
considered.reasoning: Second-difference framing captures the reallocation decision at the margin rather than the level of investment intensity, which is heavily industry-determined. Managers cut discretionary R&D first when they chase near-term capacity, so the wedge between the two accelerations is an early-warning composition signal not visible in either investment or intangible level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Intangible-Adjusted Hard Asset Expansion
considered.hypothesis: Expansion of the hard (non-intangible) balance sheet predicts low returns, but the penalty should be measured relative to a capital base that includes the firm's unbooked knowledge stock, so that knowledge-rich firms are not mistaken for overinvestors when they scale up.
considered.reasoning: The intangible theme now enters through the deflator rather than through a multiplicative rank weight, so the construct is monotone and cannot flip sign when growth is negative or when the rank is demeaned: the numerator is signed hard-asset accumulation and the denominator is a strictly positive intangible-adjusted capital base. Economically, the same dollar of tangible expansion is scored as far more aggressive for a firm with no R&D stock than for a firm whose true capital is largely off balance sheet, which is precisely the cross-theme conditioning the naive asset-growth anomaly misses.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill-Purged Knowledge Capital Tilt
considered.expression: SUB(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(intan, 0), COALESCE(gdwl, 0)), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)), at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(ppegt, at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Firms shifting their capital stock toward identifiable, non-goodwill intangibles and accumulated R&D, and away from gross physical plant, are migrating to knowledge-based production whose value is conservatively accounted and slow to be priced.
considered.reasoning: The critique is addressed by explicitly subtracting goodwill from `intan`, so the numerator captures patents, developed technology and licensed know-how plus a three-year organic R&D stock, rather than the deal premium that signals overpaying acquirers. Differencing against the change in the gross PP&E share nets out pure scale effects and isolates the tangible-versus-intangible composition shift, keeping the positive sign internally consistent with the goodwill-is-bad logic of the accepted acquisition signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expansion During Own-History R&D Retrenchment
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet expansion is most value-destructive when it coincides with the firm pulling its own R&D intensity to a five-year low, indicating that capital is being reallocated from innovation to scale precisely when management is least confident about future projects.
considered.reasoning: The second channel is a within-firm time-series position, not the cross-sectional R&D-intensity anomaly, so this is not an additive restatement of two published sorts: a chronically high-R&D firm at its own five-year R&D low is flagged just as strongly as a low-R&D firm, and a low-R&D firm that is ramping up is not flagged at all. Both components are non-negative cross-sectional ranks, so the product is monotone in each channel and cannot flip sign, and the short leg concentrates on firms simultaneously scaling assets and abandoning knowledge investment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Physical Expansion During Own-History R&D Retrenchment
considered.hypothesis: Gross plant expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has simultaneously pushed its own R&D intensity to a five-year low, indicating capital is being redirected from innovation into commoditized capacity.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the earlier validator failure by anchoring the investment leg on gross PP&E (an investment-exclusive variable) rather than total assets, while the intangible leg is a within-firm time-series position, so a chronically high-R&D firm at its own knowledge trough is flagged as strongly as a perennial non-innovator. Both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks, so the product is monotone and cannot flip sign, and the short leg concentrates on firms scaling hard capacity precisely as they disinvest in knowledge.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Plant Growth Deflated by Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
considered.hypothesis: The overinvestment penalty attaches to physical capital accumulation measured against the firm's true (tangible plus unbooked knowledge) capital base, so identical dollar plant additions are far more aggressive for firms with no R&D stock than for knowledge-rich firms.
considered.reasoning: The intangible theme enters through the deflator rather than a multiplicative weight, keeping the construct monotone with a strictly positive denominator and no sign-flip risk; this is the scaling-design repair of the earlier rejected idea, now grounded in ppent rather than assets. It isolates a clean question the archive has not answered: whether capitalizing R&D into the denominator sharpens the physical-investment penalty relative to conventional asset scaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buy Versus Build Investment Mix
considered.hypothesis: Firms that source growth by purchasing other companies rather than by building internal knowledge capital are paying acquisition premia for capability they cannot generate organically, and subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: The measure is a bounded share of the firm's total growth budget, so it avoids the sparse-goodwill and additive-rank problems of the earlier acquisition proposal while keeping the buy-versus-build contrast explicit inside a single investment budget constraint. Both zero-acquisition and zero-R&D firms are economically meaningful corners here, so the COALESCE convention is substantive rather than a coverage patch.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Idle Cash Not Converted Into Knowledge
considered.hypothesis: Large cash balances are rewarded when they fund an innovation pipeline but are an agency liability when the firm has no knowledge investment to fund, so cash-rich non-innovators underperform.
considered.reasoning: This tests a financial-slack channel distinct from the archive's external-financing winner: there the interaction was about raising capital, here it is about hoarding it without a knowledge use, which reverses the usual positive cash-R&D pricing result documented for innovative firms. The three-year cumulative R&D stock smooths lumpy annual reporting so the conditioning leg measures a sustained innovation program rather than a single-year expense.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Labor Bloat With Retreating Research
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose headcount grows faster than revenue while they simultaneously cut research intensity are scaling low-productivity labor at the same time they abandon the innovation that could justify it, and this joint divergence predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are changed relative to the flagged version: the active leg is now headcount growth in excess of sales growth, a labor-productivity deterioration measure rather than the published hiring-rate anomaly, and the gate is a within-firm decline in R&D intensity rather than the archive winner's cross-sectional low-R&D level. The mechanism is a divergence between two simultaneous input decisions — adding people while withdrawing knowledge spend — which neither the labor anomaly nor R&D intensity captures alone, and treating unreported R&D as a constant zero places non-innovators at a neutral middle rank instead of dropping them.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power
considered.hypothesis: Heavy reinvestment in physical capacity is value-destructive precisely for firms lacking an intangible moat, proxied by a persistently thin gross margin, because added capacity in a commoditized product market cannot earn rents.
considered.reasoning: This abandons both the change-of-share framing that made the flagged proposal a near-restatement of the capex-minus-R&D acceleration signal and the unstable COALESCE(xad, 0) term whose appearing-and-disappearing reporting corrupted a differenced measure. It measures the intangible side through realized pricing power — a three-year average gross margin, which is the economic output of brand and know-how rather than its accounting input — so it tests whether the moat, not the R&D line item, is what conditions the investment penalty, and it applies to the full sample including firms that never report R&D.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Serial Acquirer Without Internal Research
considered.hypothesis: Firms that have sustained a five-year program of buying growth while spending nothing on internal knowledge creation are rollups whose reported expansion is purchased rather than earned, and they persistently underperform.
considered.reasoning: The archive's Buy-Versus-Build mix delivered the largest FF5 alpha (-4.6%, t = -4.2) but a negligible Fama-MacBeth slope, which is the signature of a one-year, small-denominator ratio whose tails drive the portfolio while the cross-sectional slope is swamped by noise; replacing single-year flows with five-year cumulative spending scaled by sales gives a persistent state variable that should register cross-sectionally as well. This tests whether the buy-versus-build effect is a durable strategic-posture attribute rather than a transaction-year artifact.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory Build Without Pricing Power
considered.hypothesis: Stocking inventory faster than revenue grows is a demand-forecasting error whose cost is highest for firms without brand or product differentiation, since a commodity producer must clear excess stock through price cuts that destroy margin.
considered.reasoning: The archive's Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power was the only signal strong on both dimensions (fmb -3.1, alpha -3.0%, t = -2.9), indicating that the realized-moat gate measured by gross margin carries information the R&D expense line does not; this extends that gate to working-capital investment, an investment channel unlikely to be spanned by the FF5 investment factor built on asset growth. Netting out sales growth ensures the signal captures unwanted accumulation rather than ordinary scaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling
considered.hypothesis: Firms that expand revenue without expanding gross plant, and that have an accumulated R&D stock capable of explaining how, are monetizing unbooked knowledge capital whose scalability the market underprices.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal so far is short-side and negative-signed, leaving the long side of the intangibles story untested; this construct is deliberately built on revenue growth rather than asset growth so that it is not simply the mirror image of the FF5 investment factor, which absorbed the plant-growth signals that had strong slopes but zero alpha. The interaction is essential: sales growth without plant growth is ambiguous alone, and R&D intensity alone is a documented level effect, but jointly they identify knowledge-driven operating leverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Erratic Capex Without Knowledge Anchor
considered.hypothesis: Unstable physical investment reflects reactive, opportunity-chasing capital allocation, and it is most damaging in firms with no sustained knowledge program to give the spending strategic direction.
considered.reasoning: This introduces a second-moment investment channel absent from the archive, which has tested only levels, changes and accelerations, and the FF5 investment factor prices the level of investment rather than its instability, so the spread has a plausible route to surviving as alpha. The knowledge stock enters as the anchor that distinguishes lumpy but purposeful capacity building in innovative firms from erratic allocation in firms with no research program.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Purchased Goodwill Overhang Versus Self-Built Knowledge
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose capital base consists mostly of goodwill bought in past deals, in excess of the knowledge capital they built themselves, carry an overhang of capitalized acquisition premia that must be written down or earned back, and they underperform firms of the same size whose intangible base is self-generated.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the flow budget share entirely and moves to a stock-composition construct, which repairs the exact pathology the critic identified: the denominator is net plant plus two non-negative intangible stocks, so it is strictly positive and cannot approach zero or flip sign, and the whole measure is bounded in the interval from minus one to one without winsorizing. The economic content also changes from a single-year allocation decision to the accumulated composition of the firm's capital — purchased versus organically created intangibles measured against the physical base — which is the durable state variable the one-year Buy-Versus-Build ratio only glimpsed in transaction years.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Plant Contraction With Research Intensification
considered.hypothesis: A firm simultaneously shrinking its physical capital base and raising research intensity is executing a deliberate pivot from replicable hard assets toward knowledge capital, and because the R&D is expensed while the plant reduction is visible, reported fundamentals understate the transition and returns are subsequently high.
considered.reasoning: The critic's two objections are both structural and both fixed: the horizons are now matched — a one-year plant change against a one-year change in research intensity — and the intangible leg is a within-firm change rather than a level, so the signal is orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly and cannot be a monotone transform of it. The interaction is essential because plant contraction alone is often distress and rising research intensity alone is often a sales collapse in the denominator, whereas their conjunction identifies genuine reallocation; both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks so the product is monotone in each channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquiring Without A Moat
considered.hypothesis: Acquisitions destroy value mainly for firms that have no pricing power of their own, because a low-margin consolidator is buying scale in a commoditized market rather than acquiring differentiated capability it can monetize.
considered.reasoning: The archive shows two separately successful families — the acquisition channel, which delivers the largest alphas, and the realized-moat gate measured by sustained gross margin, which is the only conditioning variable that has produced joint cross-sectional and portfolio strength — and this crosses them for the first time. Replacing the R&D-expense gate with the margin gate also broadens the test to the majority of firms that never report R&D, where a rank on COALESCE(xrd, 0) is uninformative.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Freshly Built Plant Without Knowledge
considered.hypothesis: A high ratio of net to gross plant means the firm's physical capital is young, the cumulative product of a recent build-out, and that embedded capacity commitment is a liability rather than an asset for firms with no knowledge capital to differentiate what the capacity produces.
considered.reasoning: Capital vintage is a stock characteristic rather than an investment flow, so unlike the plant-growth signals that scored fmb -5.0 with zero alpha it is not a near-relative of the CMA asset-growth factor, which is the most plausible explanation for that earlier absorption. The interaction is necessary because young plant is neutral or good for a differentiated innovator retooling for a new product, and damaging only for a commodity producer that has locked in replicable capacity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt Against Non-Collateralizable Knowledge
considered.hypothesis: Knowledge capital cannot be pledged or liquidated, so leverage carried against an intangible-heavy asset base creates a fragile financing structure that forces pro-cyclical research cuts and depresses subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: This flips the sign convention of the archive's R&D gate — high research intensity is the risk amplifier here rather than the protective factor — which makes it a genuinely different economic claim about asset-liability matching rather than another restatement of the R&D premium. It also opens the capital-structure channel on the debt side, whereas the archive's financing evidence comes only from gross issuance flows.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill Write-Down After Acquisitive Growth
considered.hypothesis: When a serial acquirer's goodwill balance falls, management has conceded that previously capitalized acquisition premia were illusory, and because impairments are lagged and partial the market continues to over-value the remaining acquired intangibles.
considered.reasoning: This tests the realization stage of the acquisition story rather than the spending stage, a mechanism absent from the archive: the conditioning restricts the goodwill decline to firms with a documented five-year acquisition program, distinguishing genuine impairment from routine divestiture or currency translation. If the acquisition family's alpha is really about overpaid intangibles, the impairment event should time the underperformance more sharply than the spending level does.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge-Backed Gross Profit Scaling
considered.hypothesis: Firms that expand gross profit without expanding plant, and that hold a research stock capable of explaining the source of that expansion, are converting unbooked knowledge capital into rents the market has not capitalized.
considered.reasoning: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling is the archive's only joint-strength long-side result (fmb 2.4, alpha 2.8%, t 2.5), and the critic's diagnosis was that its raw sales-growth leg fights the signal because unprofitable revenue growth is itself a negative predictor; replacing sales growth with gross-profit growth keeps the asset-light scaling concept while filtering out margin-dilutive expansion. This is a targeted quality refinement of a proven mechanism rather than a new template, and it should improve both the slope and the alpha if the original leg was contaminated as diagnosed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payback On Combined Hard And Soft Investment
considered.expression: RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), LAG(SUB(sale, cogs), 3)), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), 3))
considered.hypothesis: Treating research spending as investment alongside capital expenditure, the gross profit a firm has actually generated per dollar of its total three-year hard-plus-soft outlay measures the realized productivity of its investment program, and high-payback firms are undervalued because the R&D half of the outlay was expensed and never appeared as capital.
considered.reasoning: The critic is right that the tie-mass diagnosis was wrong — Buy Versus Build was already continuous and still scored fmb -0.77 — so the correct reading is that acquisition intensity simply has no cross-sectional slope because it discriminates only within a small extreme corner, and a third denominator variant of that same construct would be wasted budget. This slot therefore moves to an untested mechanism with continuous variation across the whole sample: not the composition of investment, which the archive has probed repeatedly, but the realized payback on the two investment types pooled into one outlay, which is precisely the quantity distorted by expensing R&D and therefore the most likely source of a joint slope and alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant
considered.hypothesis: Rising gross profit per employee achieved without expanding physical plant is the fingerprint of organizational and human capital — intangible assets that never enter the balance sheet — and firms displaying it earn abnormal returns as the productivity gain proves durable.
considered.reasoning: The archive has proxied intangibles only through R&D spending, goodwill and gross margin, never through labor productivity, even though human and organizational capital is the largest unbooked intangible category for most firms; employment is broadly reported, so this avoids the zero-mass problem that flattens the R&D-gated signals. The interaction is necessary because profit per employee can rise simply through capital substitution, and requiring flat or falling gross plant isolates the intangible source from the mechanization source.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Expansion Into Eroding Margins
considered.hypothesis: Building capacity is most destructive when the firm's competitive position is actively deteriorating, so a multi-year downward margin trajectory identifies over-expansion far better than a low but stable margin level, which may simply reflect a structurally thin-margin business model.
considered.reasoning: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power is the archive's best short-side joint result, but its level-based gate necessarily confounds industry cost structure with moat erosion, and the critic flagged that it may re-express the gross-profitability anomaly. Replacing the moat level with the moat trajectory isolates that specific design choice while making the economic claim sharper: it is losing pricing power, not having thin margins, that turns investment into value destruction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Research Decay With Capacity Ramp
considered.hypothesis: An innovator whose current research spending has fallen well below its own five-year norm while it accelerates physical investment is harvesting a depleting knowledge stock, and the market continues to price the firm on an innovation profile it no longer sustains.
considered.reasoning: Every R&D leg in the archive is either a cross-sectional level or a one-year change, both of which conflate structural non-innovators with genuine retrenchers; normalizing current R&D by the firm's own five-year average makes the measure scale-free, orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly, and interpretable only within the innovator population where the depletion story applies. The capacity ramp supplies the reallocation evidence, distinguishing a firm cutting research because it is dying from one deliberately shifting its capital toward replicable hard assets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Improving Productivity Of Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
considered.hypothesis: When the capital base is measured correctly — plant plus inventory plus the capitalized research stock that accounting expenses away — an improvement in gross profit per dollar of that true capital signals rising economic productivity that reported returns on assets understate for research-intensive firms.
considered.reasoning: Rather than recombining two archive legs, this transfers the one deflator idea that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (knowledge-inclusive capital, fmb -5.0 when applied to investment) onto an entirely different quantity, profitability, where it has never been tested, and it does so as a change so the sort is not simply the gross-profitability level that RMW already prices.
